detailed_summary: This paper presents a miniaturized diamond quantum magnetometer with a 6 mm diameter endoscopic sensor head, achieving a magnetic-field sensitivity of 91 pT/√Hz with a 2 kHz measurement bandwidth in an unshielded environment. The key innovation is the use of a fused multi-core fiber bundle to separate excitation and collection paths, coupled to the diamond via a custom high-numerical-aperture micro-objective, overcoming the fluorescence collection bottleneck typical of endoscopic probes. A compact FPGA-based backend handles microwave control, lock-in detection, and real-time resonance tracking, enabling robust operation during imaging. The sensor's practical utility is demonstrated by imaging the magnetic field of a commercial lithium-ion pouch cell during charge/discharge and reconstructing depth-integrated current-density maps. This work resolves the trade-off between miniaturization and sensitivity, opening new avenues for quantum magnetometry in confined, unshielded environments such as battery diagnostics.
key_contributions: Demonstration of a 6 mm diameter endoscopic diamond magnetometer with 91 pT/√Hz sensitivity in unshielded environment.
Novel fluorescence collection scheme using a multi-core fiber bundle and custom high-NA micro-objective to overcome collection efficiency bottleneck.
Compact FPGA-based backend for real-time resonance tracking and lock-in detection, enabling robust operation during magnetic field imaging.
First application of endoscopic diamond magnetometry to image magnetic fields of a commercial lithium-ion pouch cell and reconstruct current-density maps.
methodology_analysis: The authors employ a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center ensemble in diamond as the sensing element. The diamond is optically excited via a 532 nm laser coupled through one core of a multi-core fiber bundle, and fluorescence is collected through surrounding cores, separated by a dichroic mirror. A custom micro-objective with high numerical aperture (NA ~0.8) focuses the excitation and collects fluorescence, achieving high collection efficiency despite the small probe size. Microwave delivery is via a copper wire loop integrated into the probe. The FPGA backend performs lock-in detection by modulating the microwave frequency and demodulating the fluorescence signal, with a feedback loop for real-time resonance tracking. The sensor is calibrated using a known magnetic field, and the noise floor is characterized. For battery imaging, the sensor is raster-scanned over the pouch cell surface, and the magnetic field data is inverted to reconstruct current-density maps using a depth-integrated model.
results_analysis: The sensor achieves a sensitivity of 91 pT/√Hz at 2 kHz bandwidth, with a noise floor dominated by photon shot noise. The probe diameter is 6 mm, and the total length is ~30 mm. The magnetic field imaging of a lithium-ion pouch cell during 0.5 C charge/discharge shows clear spatial variations correlated with electrode tabs and internal current distribution. The reconstructed current-density maps reveal non-uniform current flow, with peak current densities of ~100 A/m² near the tabs. The sensor's bandwidth of 2 kHz is sufficient to capture dynamic changes during cycling. The sensitivity is comparable to larger diamond magnetometers but in a significantly smaller form factor, demonstrating the effectiveness of the multi-core fiber approach.
strengths: Achieves high sensitivity (91 pT/√Hz) in a compact endoscopic form factor (6 mm diameter), resolving a key trade-off.
Innovative use of multi-core fiber bundle and custom micro-objective to enhance fluorescence collection efficiency.
Real-time resonance tracking via FPGA enables robust operation in unshielded environments without active magnetic shielding.
Practical demonstration on a commercial battery, showing immediate applicability to energy storage diagnostics.
limitations: The sensitivity is still an order of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art bulky diamond magnetometers (e.g., <10 pT/√Hz).
The probe length (~30 mm) may still be too large for some endoscopic applications (e.g., deep brain imaging).
The current-density reconstruction relies on a depth-integrated model, which may not capture 3D current distributions accurately.
connections_to_research: This work directly advances quantum sensing using NV centers in diamond, a core topic in quantum physics. It demonstrates practical miniaturization of a quantum magnetometer, addressing the challenge of transitioning laboratory quantum sensors to real-world applications. The use of NV centers for magnetic field imaging aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics and its applications. The paper also touches on information theory through the lock-in detection and real-time feedback, which are relevant to quantum measurement and control.
overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant engineering achievement in quantum magnetometry, successfully miniaturizing a diamond NV sensor to an endoscopic form factor while maintaining high sensitivity. The multi-core fiber bundle approach is a clever solution to the fluorescence collection bottleneck. The demonstration on a commercial battery is compelling and highlights the sensor's practical utility. While the sensitivity is not record-breaking, the trade-off between size and performance is well-balanced. The work is novel, well-executed, and likely to inspire further developments in portable quantum sensors for industrial and biomedical applications.
